summary:
Sol Stroll is a go/no-go briefing for a single real Marswalk in Gale Crater, built for the NASA Space Apps challenge to create a layered Marswalk map. We developed a work-in-progress web prototype that places a boxwork route on a flat, top-down map and layers three kinds of data: orbital imagery with elevation, atmospheric readings from Curiosity, and radiation and space weather. A five-check verdict covers solar storms, walk time, distance from base, daylight and temperature, and it openly shows anything it hasn’t checked. Route limits are based on NASA’s suit planning figures, which we label as planning assumptions.
It matters because Mars crews can’t rely on a live link to Earth. Sol Stroll keeps working offline from saved data, clearly dated so the crew knows how fresh it is. It can also run on a budget Chromebook, so the low computing demand makes wide use for training and rehearsal practical, and a future suit display plausible.
details:
SOL STROLL: KNOW BEFORE YOU GO

A go / no-go briefing for one real Marswalk, built from NASA mission data.

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Sol Stroll is a briefing for one real Marswalk in the boxwork region of Mount Sharp, Gale Crater. It answers the question a crew faces every morning: should we go out today? It has three views, switched from the top bar:

- Map: HiRISE and CTX orbital imagery, with elevation contours, a grid, place names and colour imagery as layers. It shows the safest walking path between the chosen stops, coloured by difficulty, with warnings at steep ground, sand and the biggest climb. A camera badge at each stop opens what Curiosity's navigation camera saw from that spot, in eight directions. The day's verdict sits in a pop-up beside the map.

- Briefing: the verdict and every check behind it, then distance, climb, walking time and difficulty for each section, the tasks at each stop, the dangers and a packing list.

- Weather: Curiosity's latest published readings, charts of temperature and pressure, and NASA space weather.

The path is found with an A* search over a network of 263 drives Curiosity actually made, leaving out ground steeper than NASA's 20° planning figure. It never routes across ground no rover crossed, because orbital elevation data is too coarse to judge slopes at walking scale.

The verdict uses five checks:

1. Whether NASA forecast a solar storm reaching Mars that day (DONKI).

2. NASA's 8-hour walk limit.

3. NASA's 2 km walk-back limit.

4. Daylight.

5. How unusual the day's temperature is compared with other sols at the same season, across 14 years of Curiosity's records.

Any past sol can be typed in and judged. The same walk is Go on sol 4711, Caution on sol 2100 (the 2018 dust storm) and No-go on sol 1947, when NASA forecast a solar storm hitting Mars.

"Begin journey" runs a simulated walk for a tablet. On arrival at each stop, the walker compares the ground with Curiosity's photos and confirms they are there with a hold-and-slide. A simulated helmet visor shows only the critical readings.

MEETING THE CHALLENGE

1. A science goal at a well-studied location

- Boxwork is a network of low ridges about 1 to 2 metres tall with sandy hollows between them, on the slopes of Mount Sharp (NASA/JPL).

- The Nodule site stop matches a real open question. NASA reported that nodules were found along ridge walls and in the hollows, not near the central fractures as expected, and scientists are still unsure how they formed.

- HiRISE imaged the boxwork from orbit, and Curiosity photographed it at ground level.

2. At least three data types, layered

- Optical and topographic: HiRISE and CTX imagery with contours from the HiRISE elevation model, through NASA Mars Trek.

- Atmospheric: Curiosity REMS daily readings of air and ground temperature, pressure, ultraviolet index, and sunrise and sunset.

- Space weather: NASA DONKI, whose WSA-ENLIL model runs estimate when solar storms arrive at Mars. These are forecasts, not radiation measurements at the surface.

- Ground-level imagery: 120 Curiosity navigation camera frames, eight directions at each of 15 stops.

- Rover tracks: Curiosity's waypoints and traverse, used for the path search and the slope warnings.

3. Astronaut safety

Every limit is NASA's own, cited in the app, and marked "lunar" where it is a lunar figure. The few rules that are ours are labelled "ours". The fifth check flags an unusual day; it is not a temperature limit, because no Mars suit limit is published. DONKI notes that its content is experimental research information, and the app labels it as a forecast.

4. Suited mobility and a route that avoids obstacles

- The limits come from NASA's EVA-EXP-0042: walks of up to 8 hours, slopes up to 20°, traverses up to 2 km from base, at 2 km/h.

- These are lunar planning figures. NASA's own document says Mars walking ranges are still "forward work", and the 2 km figure is marked "to be reviewed" in NASA slides, so we call it a planning assumption.

- Slope comes from how far Curiosity tilted when it drove there. It is a hint at slope, not a measurement.

- The default walk is 652 m and 202 m out (854 m), 854 m back, 1,708 m round trip, with about 108 m of climbing. The biggest single climb is +56 m, and the walk never goes more than 0.5 km from the start.

5. Built for no signal

One-way signal delay between Earth and Mars ranges from about 3 to 22 minutes, and every 26 months a solar conjunction causes a communications blackout of about two weeks.

- The page checks its link to NASA every 30 seconds and switches by itself; nobody has to choose.

- After the first visit, the whole site (about 18 MB, including map tiles and ground photos) is saved on the device, so it reopens with no signal.

- NASA map tiles the device has already viewed are kept and shown again, and the latest space weather it read is kept with its date.

- With no signal, the top bar reads "NO SIGNAL · DATA TO 15 NOV 2026", so the crew always knows how fresh the information is. When signal returns, the page goes live again by itself.

6. Lightweight and low-cost to run

- The first load is 1.6 MB, measured at a 1366 × 768 screen. Heavy work, such as building the path network and preparing the map tiles, is done in advance by scripts, not in the browser.

- The team tested it on an Acer Chromebook Spin 511 (R752TN): a budget education laptop with an Intel Celeron processor, 4 GB of RAM, integrated Intel UHD Graphics 600, 32 GB of storage and an 11.6-inch 1366 × 768 touch screen.

- It is a static site on GitHub Pages, with no server to maintain, and it reads public NASA services.

- Because it runs on cheap, common devices, crews could rehearse routes and go / no-go decisions on ordinary laptops or tablets before a mission.

- Running well on a Chromebook shows low computing demand. It does not show the software could run inside a spacesuit, which would need its own hardware, radiation tolerance and certification.

7. Why a flat map and not a 3D globe

A single Marswalk covers a few hundred metres. Mars has a radius of about 3,396 km, so by our calculation the ground curves away by only about 4 cm over the 520 m to the walk's furthest point, and about 0.6 m over NASA's 2 km limit. The source imagery is already stored as flat map projections, and at full resolution it is huge: the USGS Gale Crater orthophoto mosaic is 23 GB. 3D globes are also heavy on graphics hardware. Sol Stroll stores the walk area and the whole crater in about 12 MB of imagery, which runs on integrated graphics and works offline. A 3D preview limited to the route corridor is a possible later addition.

WHAT IS NOT BUILT YET

- Curiosity's ground photos are not yet shown side by side with the orbital view.

- There is no guided replay of a storm. Any past sol can be typed in, but nothing steps through it.

- Radiation dose on the ground is not shown. One published estimate puts surface exposure at about 125 mSv a year; we would add it only with a properly sourced figure.

- Curiosity's published weather record ends on 25 Aug 2026, so it is described as "latest published", never as live.

BENEFITS

- One decision instead of many tools: the crew gets one answer, with the evidence behind it, instead of combining orbital maps, weather records and space weather alerts by hand.

- It works without Earth, and always shows how old its data is.

- It runs on cheap hardware and is free to host.

- It is honest about what it knows. No temperature, ultraviolet or radiation limits are invented, because none are published for a Mars suit.

INTENDED IMPACT

To show that NASA's existing mission data can already answer the question a first Mars crew will face every morning, and to give planners and trainees a free tool to rehearse it. The method is not tied to this site: any place with orbital imagery, rover tracks and a weather record could get the same briefing.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- The question is different: the entries we reviewed plan a route; Sol Stroll decides whether to walk it, and the answer changes with the date.

- Real bad days can be replayed against the plan, such as the 2018 dust storm and the 2017 solar storm.

- The walker confirms their position against what the rover actually saw at each stop.

- It is designed for the communications gaps of a real Mars mission, rather than assuming a constant link.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Safety: NASA's published limits wherever they exist, cited in the app.

- Validity: every number traceable to a dataset, with measured, derived and assumed values labelled differently.

- Connectivity: signal delay and blackouts.

- Hardware: a light page on a low-cost laptop.

- Gloves and dust: large touch targets, and hold-and-slide instead of single taps for actions that matter.

- Accessibility: keyboard use and colour contrast.

- Scope: one real site done properly instead of a whole planet done roughly.

TOOLS

- Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules, type-checked with JSDoc, no framework, no build step); Python for data preparation.

- Libraries: Leaflet 1.9.4 for the map; Pillow and PyYAML in Python.

- Testing: 91 automated tests with Node's test runner, Python unittest for the path search, and Playwright with headless Chromium for checking the page in dark and light themes at phone, tablet and desktop widths.

- Hosting and version control: GitHub Pages, Git and GitHub.

- Design: Figma, and a written design system with dark and light themes.

- Hardware: Acer Chromebook Spin 511 (R752TN).

- AI: generative AI (Claude Code) was used to help write and check code and documentation.

NASA DATA USED

- MRO HiRISE mosaic, via Mars Trek: https://trek.nasa.gov/tiles/Mars/EQ/curiosity_hirise_mosaic/1.0.0/WMTSCapabilities.xml

- MRO CTX mosaic of Gale Crater, via Mars Trek: https://trek.nasa.gov/tiles/Mars/EQ/curiosity_ctx_mosaic/1.0.0/WMTSCapabilities.xml

- HiRISE elevation model, via Mars Trek: https://trek.nasa.gov/tiles/Mars/EQ/Gale_DEM_SMG_1m/1.0.0/WMTSCapabilities.xml

- Mars Trek portal: https://trek.nasa.gov/mars/

- HiRISE colour mosaic, from Curiosity's location map: https://mars.nasa.gov/mmgis-maps/MSL/Layers/MSL_Gale_HiRISE-LRGB_78quads/

- Curiosity waypoints: https://mars.nasa.gov/mmgis-maps/MSL/Layers/json/MSL_waypoints.json

- Curiosity traverse: https://mars.nasa.gov/mmgis-maps/MSL/Layers/json/MSL_traverse.json

- Curiosity place names: https://mars.nasa.gov/mmgis-maps/MSL/Layers/json/MSL_SurfaceSites.json

- Curiosity REMS weather: https://mars.nasa.gov/rss/api/?feed=weather&category=msl&feedtype=json

- Curiosity raw images (ground photos): https://mars.nasa.gov/msl/multimedia/raw-images/

- NASA DONKI space weather: https://ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/tools/DONKI

NASA DOCUMENTS CITED

- EVA-EXP-0042 Rev B: https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/eva-exp-0042_xeva_system_con_ops_rev_b_final_dtd_10192020_ref_doc.pdf

- NASA-STD-3001 Vol 1 Rev C: https://standards.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/standards/NASA/C//nasa-std-3001-vol-1-rev-c-signature.pdf

- Boxwork findings: https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasas-curiosity-rover-sees-martian-spiderwebs-up-close/

- Boxwork exploration: https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasas-curiosity-mars-rover-starts-unpacking-boxwork-formations/

- Curiosity's proposed path up Mount Sharp: https://science.nasa.gov/resource/curiositys-proposed-path-up-mount-sharp/

- Lunar traverse precedent: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20210026296/downloads/Scoville%20Final%20presentation%20-%20compressed.pptx.pdf

OTHER SOURCES

- JMARS (layering precedent): https://jmars.mars.asu.edu/what-jmars

- USGS Gale Crater orthophoto mosaic: https://astrogeology.usgs.gov/search/map/mars_msl_gale_merged_orthophoto_mosaic_25cm

- Communication delays and conjunction (Planetary Society): https://planetary.org/articles/challenges-facing-the-human-exploration-of-mars

- Chromebook specifications (Bechtle datasheet): https://media.bechtle.com/asrc/180712/1c4b3d4ee288fc9434f5175bf56070570/c3/-/8319f1c1932e4363917ea19e19007510/acer-chromebook-spin-511-celeron-4-32gb-datablad-1

- Open-source software: Leaflet (https://leafletjs.com/), fonts Inter, JetBrains Mono and Space Grotesk, and Material Symbols icons (https://fonts.google.com/)

Made for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.
